description: The layers the substrate's existing compiler_theory + llvm_passes + llvm_ir Mts didn't cover. Front-end (lexer, parser, AST, type checking). Mid-end advanced optimisations (inlining, loop opts, alias analysis). Back-end (register allocation, instruction selection, scheduling). JIT specifics (tracing, method, tiered, OSR). Modern compiler infrastructure (MLIR, Clang, Rust MIR, GCC GIMPLE). The substrate already understands LLVM IR + 72 IR passes; this Mt fills in everything around that core.
category_inheritance: genlMt → compiler_theory. Specialisation: this Mt's concepts are concrete compiler-pipeline mechanisms that instantiate the compiler_theory framework. Equivalence vocabulary (denotational, algebraic, extensional, cost, referential_transparency) applies directly. Each rule's soundness_category names the equivalence-kind it preserves.

concepts.name: lexer
concepts.definition: Tokeniser: scans source code character-by-character, groups into tokens (identifiers, keywords, literals, operators). Output: token stream.
concepts.why: Separates lexical structure from grammar. Parser doesn't see whitespace, comments, or character-level details. Standard tools: lex, flex, hand-written, or generated. Lexer-parser split is the foundational front-end architecture.

concepts.name: regular_language
concepts.definition: Languages recognisable by finite automata. Lexer tokens are typically regular: identifiers, integers, keywords match regex patterns.
concepts.why: Tokens have no recursive structure (no nested parens in an identifier). Regular suffices, and finite automata are efficient (linear-time scan). Distinguishing regular from context-free is what makes the lexer-parser split work.

concepts.name: finite_automaton
concepts.definition: State machine with finite states + deterministic transitions on input characters. DFA (deterministic) or NFA (nondeterministic).
concepts.why: Lexers compile to DFAs via subset construction from NFA. Each state encodes 'what we've matched so far'. The transition table is the lexer's compiled form. Linear-time scanning per input character.

concepts.name: longest_match_rule
concepts.definition: When multiple tokens could match starting at a position, take the longest. 'if' is a keyword but 'iffy' is an identifier.
concepts.why: Without this rule, lexer would be ambiguous. Standard lexer behavior: scan as far as the DFA allows, then commit to that token. Edge cases (== vs =) handled by this rule.

concepts.name: parser
concepts.definition: Builds an AST from token stream by matching against a grammar. Top-down (LL, recursive descent) or bottom-up (LR, SLR).
concepts.why: Imposes structure on linear token sequence. AST captures the program's hierarchical meaning. Parser correctness depends on grammar being unambiguous for the parsing algorithm.

concepts.name: context_free_grammar
concepts.definition: Set of production rules N → α where N is a non-terminal and α is a sequence of terminals and non-terminals. Captures nested/recursive structure.
concepts.why: Programming languages are CFGs (or close). Nesting (matched parens, nested blocks) requires CFG power; regular grammars can't count. Defines what programs are syntactically valid.

concepts.name: AST_abstract_syntax_tree
concepts.definition: Tree representation of syntactic structure: each node is a construct (expression, statement, declaration). Children are subconstructs.
concepts.why: Concrete syntax (parentheses, punctuation) discarded; structural meaning preserved. AST is the unit that semantic analysis + optimization + code gen operate on. Compiler's first 'understood' representation.

concepts.name: recursive_descent_parser
concepts.definition: One function per grammar non-terminal. Each function tries to match its production, recursively calling other functions for sub-productions.
concepts.why: Hand-written, readable, good error messages. Predictive (LL(1)) for unambiguous grammars; backtracking for ambiguous. Used by Clang (C++), Rust's parser, many production compilers — speed + control matter at scale.

concepts.name: LL_parsing
concepts.definition: Left-to-right scan, leftmost derivation. LL(k) needs k tokens of lookahead. LL(1) is the simplest practical case.
concepts.why: Top-down parsing. Can be implemented as recursive descent. Cannot handle left-recursive grammars directly (requires rewriting). Used in many hand-written parsers.

concepts.name: LR_parsing
concepts.definition: Left-to-right scan, rightmost derivation. Bottom-up: shift tokens onto stack, reduce by applying productions. LR(0), SLR, LALR, LR(1) variants.
concepts.why: Strictly more powerful than LL: handles left-recursion, ambiguous-looking grammars naturally. Implementation: parser tables computed from grammar. Used by yacc, Bison, GLR parsers.

concepts.name: shift_reduce_conflict
concepts.definition: Parser state can either shift the next token OR reduce by a completed production. Conflict means grammar ambiguity.
concepts.why: Classic problem in LR parsing (e.g., dangling else). Resolved by precedence rules, grammar rewriting, or convention (default: shift). Tooling reports them as warnings; ignoring them produces wrong parse.

concepts.name: PEG_parser
concepts.definition: Parsing Expression Grammar. Like CFG but with ordered alternatives (a / b means try a first, then b). Inherently unambiguous.
concepts.why: Simpler than LR for some grammars. Used in Python's PEG parser (Python 3.9+ replaced LL(1)). The ordered choice gives clear semantics for what 'matches first' means.

concepts.name: packrat_parsing
concepts.definition: PEG implementation with memoisation: each (rule, position) pair computed once. Linear time at cost of O(n) space per rule.
concepts.why: Eliminates exponential blow-up from PEG's backtracking. Trade memory for time. Used in some PEG implementations; less common in production compilers due to memory cost.

concepts.name: error_recovery
concepts.definition: Parser strategy when encountering invalid input: discard tokens until a synchronisation point (semicolon, brace), resume parsing.
concepts.why: Compiler should report many errors per run, not stop at first. Recovery quality affects developer experience. Recursive-descent parsers (Clang, Rust) often have hand-tuned recovery; generated parsers struggle.

concepts.name: type_checking
concepts.definition: Static analysis verifying that operations are applied to compatible types. Traversal of AST checking each node against typing rules.
concepts.why: Catches errors before runtime. Type checker IS the language's static semantics. Generates errors for ill-typed programs; annotates AST with inferred types for later passes.

concepts.name: type_inference
concepts.definition: Deriving types without explicit annotations. Constraint generation + unification. Hindley-Milner (HM) is the foundational algorithm.
concepts.why: Lets programmers write 'let x = expr' without 'int x = ...'. Languages with HM-style inference: ML, Haskell, OCaml, Rust (modified), TypeScript (extended). Polymorphism via let-generalisation.

concepts.name: hindley_milner
concepts.definition: Classic type inference algorithm (Damas-Milner). Generates type constraints, solves via unification, generalises let-bound types.
concepts.why: Proves: complete inference for prenex polymorphic let-bindings. Foundation of ML-family languages. Modifications for subtyping (Rust), gradual typing (TypeScript), higher-rank (Haskell).

concepts.name: unification
concepts.definition: Find substitution that makes two types equal. Walk both types in parallel, unify sub-parts. Type variables get bound to concrete types.
concepts.why: Core of HM type inference. Robinson's algorithm: O(n α(n)) with union-find. The mechanism by which constraints get solved. Used beyond compilers (Prolog, theorem provers).

concepts.name: subtyping
concepts.definition: Type A is a subtype of B if values of A can be used wherever B is expected. Java's class hierarchy, structural subtyping (Go interfaces, TypeScript), Rust's lifetime subtyping.
concepts.why: Captures 'is-a' relationships. Type checker must handle subtyping in unification (e.g., narrowing). Complicates HM significantly — Rust's type system is HM + lifetime constraints + subtyping + traits.

concepts.name: function_inlining
concepts.definition: Replace a function call with the called function's body, substituting arguments.
concepts.why: Eliminates call overhead. Enables further optimisations (constant propagation across the call boundary). Heuristic: small + hot callees. Excessive inlining bloats code; insufficient leaves performance on the table.

concepts.name: loop_invariant_code_motion
concepts.definition: LICM: hoist computations that don't depend on the loop's induction variable out of the loop.
concepts.why: Per-iteration cost → one-time cost. Classic optimisation; substantial speedup on hot loops. The hoisting must respect dependencies; complicated by aliasing.

concepts.name: loop_unrolling
concepts.definition: Duplicate the loop body N times, decrease iteration count proportionally. Reduces branch overhead, enables further per-body optimisations.
concepts.why: Branch overhead amortises across body replicas. Modern CPUs with good branch prediction benefit less; SIMD unrolling exposes vector parallelism. LLVM's loop unroller is tuned per target.

concepts.name: loop_vectorisation
concepts.definition: Convert scalar loop to SIMD operations: one instruction operating on N lanes. Requires no inter-iteration dependencies.
concepts.why: Nx speedup on data-parallel loops. LLVM's loop vectorizer + SLP vectorizer handle this. Critical for HPC, ML, media. The 'easy' parallelism — auto-vectorisation succeeds when alias analysis can prove independence.

concepts.name: alias_analysis
concepts.definition: Determine whether two pointers might point to the same memory location. Essential precondition for many optimisations.
concepts.why: Without it, compiler must conservatively assume any two memory operations might conflict — forbidding reordering. Andersen's, Steensgaard's, flow-sensitive variants trade precision for cost.

concepts.name: andersen_alias_analysis
concepts.definition: Inclusion-based pointer analysis. Subset constraints: pts(p) ⊇ pts(q) when q is assigned to p. Solves to fixed point.
concepts.why: More precise than Steensgaard's at cost of O(n³) worst case. Used in production for moderate-size programs. Tracks 'which abstract locations can each pointer reach'.

concepts.name: steensgaard_alias_analysis
concepts.definition: Equality-based: if p and q can alias, all things they point to are merged into one equivalence class. O(n α(n)).
concepts.why: Much faster than Andersen — near-linear via union-find. Less precise (over-approximates aliasing). Used in early or fast-pass settings; Andersen for later/precise passes.

concepts.name: escape_analysis
concepts.definition: Determines whether an object's lifetime escapes its allocation scope (stored in a field, returned, passed to a function).
concepts.why: If object doesn't escape, can stack-allocate instead of heap-allocate (eliminates GC pressure). Java JITs, Go compiler, V8 do this. Significant performance + memory benefit on short-lived objects.

concepts.name: tail_call_optimisation
concepts.definition: When a function's last action is a call, reuse the current stack frame instead of pushing a new one.
concepts.why: Recursion equivalent to iteration; deep recursion doesn't blow the stack. Functional languages (Scheme, Haskell, OCaml) require TCO. C/C++ compilers do it opportunistically; Python explicitly doesn't.

concepts.name: ssa_form
concepts.definition: Static Single Assignment: each variable is assigned exactly once. PHI nodes merge values from different control-flow predecessors.
concepts.why: Simplifies many analyses: def-use chains are explicit, dataflow is straightforward. LLVM IR is in SSA form. Conversion from non-SSA via dominance frontiers (Cytron's algorithm).

concepts.name: register_allocation
concepts.definition: Assign virtual registers (LLVM IR has unlimited) to physical machine registers (x86_64 has ~16). Spill to stack if no register available.
concepts.why: IR has infinite virtual registers; CPU has finite physical ones. RA is the back-end's hardest problem. Quality directly affects generated code performance. Spilling is expensive (memory access vs register).

concepts.name: graph_coloring_RA
concepts.definition: Construct interference graph (nodes are values; edges connect values live at the same time). Colour with K colours (K = available registers). NP-hard in general.
concepts.why: Optimal-ish solution. Used by GCC, classical compilers. Variants (Chaitin-Briggs, IRC) refine the coloring + spill strategy. NP-hardness handled by heuristics + spilling.

concepts.name: linear_scan_RA
concepts.definition: Sort live ranges by start time. Walk through; at each program point, assign register or spill the longest-remaining live range.
concepts.why: Faster than graph coloring: O(n log n). Lower-quality code (sometimes ~10% worse). Used by JITs (V8, LuaJIT) where compile time dominates. LLVM's old default; replaced by Greedy.

concepts.name: greedy_RA
concepts.definition: LLVM's modern register allocator. Live range splitting + priority-based allocation + iterative refinement.
concepts.why: Quality close to graph coloring + speed close to linear scan. Default in LLVM since 2011. Handles register pressure adaptively via live range splitting.

concepts.name: instruction_selection
concepts.definition: Map IR operations to target ISA instructions. Pattern-match IR tree (or DAG) against patterns; emit matched instructions.
concepts.why: IR ops are abstract (add); ISA ops are concrete (add r1, r2, r3 vs LEA r1, [r2 + r3]). Pattern matching picks the best instruction sequence. Quality affects code density + speed.

concepts.name: burs_bottom_up_rewriting
concepts.definition: Bottom-up rewriting system: pattern match the IR DAG against rewrite rules. Each rule has a cost; chooses minimum-cost tiling.
concepts.why: Optimal DAG tiling via dynamic programming. LLVM's SelectionDAG, GCC's RTL use variants. Costs reflect target-specific instruction prices.

concepts.name: instruction_scheduling
concepts.definition: Reorder instructions to minimise pipeline stalls + maximise instruction-level parallelism.
concepts.why: Same set of instructions, different orderings, different performance. List scheduling, software pipelining are standard techniques. Most beneficial on in-order CPUs; modern OoO does much of this in hardware.

concepts.name: list_scheduling
concepts.definition: Maintain ready list of instructions whose dependencies are satisfied. Pick the highest-priority ready instruction.
concepts.why: Greedy heuristic that works well in practice. Priority functions consider latency, critical path, resource conflicts. Standard technique in LLVM, GCC, ICC.

concepts.name: software_pipelining
concepts.definition: Overlap iterations of a loop: while iteration N executes instruction K, iteration N+1 executes instruction K-1.
concepts.why: Exposes ILP across iteration boundaries. Critical for in-order CPUs (DSPs, VLIW). Modulo scheduling is the main algorithm. Less critical on modern OoO superscalar CPUs.

concepts.name: JIT_just_in_time
concepts.definition: Compile code at runtime rather than ahead of time. Trade compilation latency for runtime performance.
concepts.why: Enables: speculative optimisations (deoptimise on assumption violation), runtime type specialisation (V8's hidden classes), profile-guided code generation. Used in JVM, V8, LuaJIT, .NET, PyPy.

concepts.name: method_JIT
concepts.definition: Compile entire functions when they get hot. JVM HotSpot's C1/C2, V8's TurboFan, .NET RyuJIT.
concepts.why: Whole-function optimisation: inlining, register allocation, loop opts. Compilation latency is the cost. Mitigated by tiered compilation: cheap C1 first, expensive C2 only for very hot code.

concepts.name: tracing_JIT
concepts.definition: Compile hot execution traces (a sequence of instructions actually executed). LuaJIT, TraceMonkey (early Firefox JS), PyPy.
concepts.why: Optimise the common case observed at runtime. Trace cuts across function boundaries → strong inlining. Cost: trace exits (guards) deoptimise to interpreter; bad guard placement kills performance.

concepts.name: tiered_compilation
concepts.definition: Multiple compilation levels: interpret → cheap JIT (Java's C1, V8's Sparkplug) → expensive JIT (C2, TurboFan). Functions promote as they get hot.
concepts.why: Trade compilation latency for steady-state performance. Cold code stays interpreted (cheap); hot code gets expensive optimisation. The standard production JIT design since the 2010s.

concepts.name: OSR_on_stack_replacement
concepts.definition: Transition from interpreted/lower-tier code to higher-tier code WITHIN a running function (e.g., inside a hot loop).
concepts.why: Hot loop in a cold function would otherwise run interpreted forever. OSR copies the interpreter's stack frame to the compiled frame mid-execution. Tricky to implement; critical for JIT performance on long-running loops.

concepts.name: deoptimisation
concepts.definition: Transition from compiled code back to interpreter, typically because a runtime assumption was violated.
concepts.why: JITs make optimistic assumptions (inline this monomorphic call, this loop iterates >100 times). Violations require deopt: reconstruct interpreter state from compiled state. Inverse of OSR.

concepts.name: inline_cache
concepts.definition: Per-call-site cache mapping observed receiver type → resolved method. Avoids virtual dispatch lookup on repeat calls.
concepts.why: JavaScript and Smalltalk's massive runtime speedup. Monomorphic IC: one type, direct call. Polymorphic IC: small dispatch table. Megamorphic: fall back to slow lookup. V8's foundational performance technique.

concepts.name: hidden_class
concepts.definition: V8's runtime data structure tracking the layout of an object based on the property set + order. Shared between objects with identical history.
concepts.why: Lets dynamic JavaScript objects act like static C++ objects at the CPU level: field access is a fixed offset. Inline caches reference hidden classes. The core of V8's performance.

concepts.name: profile_guided_optimisation
concepts.definition: PGO: collect runtime profile (branch frequencies, call counts), then recompile using that data to inform optimisation choices.
concepts.why: Compile-time guesses replaced with runtime measurements. Inline hot calls, layout code for predicted branches, avoid optimising cold paths. 5-25% speedup typical on real workloads.

concepts.name: speculative_optimisation
concepts.definition: JIT optimisations based on runtime observations (typed property accesses, monomorphic calls) that can be invalidated.
concepts.why: Aggressive: assume the common case, deopt on violation. V8, HotSpot, LuaJIT do this extensively. Without speculation, dynamic languages would be 10-100x slower.

concepts.name: MLIR
concepts.definition: Multi-Level Intermediate Representation. LLVM project's IR-of-IRs: a single framework for representing multiple dialects (ML, polyhedral, GPU, etc.) at different abstraction levels.
concepts.why: Compilers need many IRs (high-level for source semantics, mid-level for optimisation, low-level for code gen). MLIR provides one infrastructure for all. Used in TensorFlow's XLA, PyTorch 2.0's Inductor, IREE.

concepts.name: MLIR_dialect
concepts.definition: A specific instantiation of MLIR for a particular domain or abstraction level: linalg (linear algebra), affine (loops), scf (structured control flow), gpu, llvm dialect.
concepts.why: Each dialect captures domain-specific structure. Lowering pipeline progressively rewrites from high-level dialect to lower until reaching the LLVM dialect → LLVM IR → assembly.

concepts.name: Clang_frontend
concepts.definition: LLVM's C/C++/Objective-C front-end. Hand-written recursive-descent parser, AST representation, type checker, codegen to LLVM IR.
concepts.why: Production C++ front-end. Used by Apple, Google, FreeBSD as the system compiler. Modular design lets tools (clang-format, clang-tidy, static analyzers) reuse the front-end without re-implementing.

concepts.name: GCC_GIMPLE
concepts.definition: GCC's tree-based IR. SSA form, three-address operations. Sits between Generic (source-level tree) and RTL (target-aware).
concepts.why: Multi-level IR was GCC's approach before MLIR existed. Generic → GIMPLE → RTL pipeline. Each level enables different optimisations. Generic's source-level structure for high-level opts; GIMPLE's SSA for mid-level; RTL's machine-aware for back-end.

concepts.name: Rust_MIR
concepts.definition: Rust's Mid-level IR. Control-flow graph of statements + terminators. Borrow checker operates on MIR; optimisation passes apply before lowering to LLVM IR.
concepts.why: Bridges Rust's HIR (high-level, type-checked) and LLVM IR. Borrow check needs a specific shape; MIR is that shape. Rust-specific opts (move-tracking, panic elision) happen here.

concepts.name: WebAssembly
concepts.definition: Bytecode + stack machine model. Designed as a compilation target for C/C++/Rust. Runs in browsers, embedded systems, edge compute.
concepts.why: Portable, sandboxed, fast. Compilers target Wasm; runtime (V8, Wasmtime) JITs or AOT-compiles it. Used to bring native-language code to browsers (Photoshop, Figma, Google Earth) + edge compute (Cloudflare Workers).

concepts.name: GraalVM
concepts.definition: Oracle's polyglot VM. Optimising JIT (Graal compiler) for JVM + Truffle interpreter framework for other languages.
concepts.why: Java compiled by Graal often beats HotSpot's C2 on some workloads. Truffle's partial evaluation lets Ruby, Python, JavaScript share Graal's optimisations. Important research vehicle.

concepts.name: compiler_explorer
concepts.definition: Godbolt's compiler explorer (godbolt.org). Web-based tool showing assembly output for any language + compiler + version. The 'show me the code' tool of the 2020s.
concepts.why: Made compiler output instantly inspectable. Drove broader appreciation of compiler quality differences (gcc vs clang vs icc), enables learning + debugging optimisation behaviour. Generation of programmers grew up using it.

concepts.name: intermediate_representation
concepts.definition: Compiler's internal representation of the program between source and machine code. Designed for analysis + transformation.
concepts.why: Source is human-friendly; machine code is target-specific. IR is the transformation substrate. Multi-level IR (Generic → GIMPLE in GCC, MLIR dialects in modern compilers) handles different abstraction needs at different stages.

concepts.name: three_address_code
concepts.definition: IR where each instruction has at most 3 operands: dst = src1 op src2. LLVM IR, GIMPLE all use this form.
concepts.why: Simple, regular structure. Each instruction does one operation. Easier to analyse + transform than tree-style source. Universal across modern compilers.

concepts.name: control_flow_graph
concepts.definition: Directed graph: nodes are basic blocks, edges are possible jumps. Each function has a CFG.
concepts.why: Many analyses are dataflow problems on the CFG. Dominators, post-dominators, loops all derived from CFG structure. The structural representation of control flow.

concepts.name: dataflow_analysis
concepts.definition: Compute properties at each program point (reaching definitions, live variables, available expressions). Iterate to fixed point.
concepts.why: Foundation of many optimisations. Live variable analysis powers register allocation; reaching definitions powers constant propagation. The lattice + transfer function framework is universal.

concepts.name: dominator_tree
concepts.definition: Node X dominates Y if every path from entry to Y passes through X. Tree structure: each node's parent is its immediate dominator.
concepts.why: Required for SSA conversion (dominance frontiers determine PHI placement). Loop detection. Common subexpression elimination. The structural backbone of many compiler analyses.

concepts.name: phi_node
concepts.definition: SSA construct merging values from different predecessor blocks. φ(v1 from B1, v2 from B2): result is v1 if execution came from B1, v2 from B2.
concepts.why: Lets SSA handle control flow merges (after if-else, at loop entry). Conceptually executed at block entry. Implementation: parallel copies inserted on incoming edges. Foundational SSA mechanism.

concepts.name: abstract_interpretation
concepts.definition: Framework for static analysis: execute the program over an abstract domain (intervals, signs, polyhedra) rather than concrete values.
concepts.why: Theoretical foundation of many analyses. Soundness proof via Galois connection between concrete and abstract semantics. Used in compiler optimisations + verification (Polyspace, Astrée).

concepts.name: polyhedral_optimisation
concepts.definition: Loop nests modelled as polyhedra; transformations (tiling, parallelisation, vectorisation) are affine mappings on those polyhedra.
concepts.why: Provably optimal for affine loops. Used in GCC's Graphite, LLVM's Polly, Pluto. Powerful for HPC + ML workloads. Complex to implement; expensive analysis.

concepts.name: ahead_of_time_compilation
concepts.definition: AOT: compile to machine code before deployment. Standard for C/C++/Rust. Some JIT languages have AOT alternatives (Java's GraalVM Native Image, JS via static binding).
concepts.why: No runtime compilation cost. Faster startup. Smaller memory footprint (no compiler/profile in memory). Trade-off: no runtime profile information; speculative opts impossible.

concepts.name: LLVM_IR_to_assembly
concepts.definition: LLVM's backend: IR → SelectionDAG → MachineFunction → assembly. Multi-stage: instruction selection, register allocation, scheduling, asm emission.
concepts.why: The actual generation of native code. Different targets share LLVM's mid-end IR but have target-specific selectors + register sets. Adding a new architecture means writing target-specific backend phases.

concepts.name: stack_frame
concepts.definition: Per-function stack region: parameters, locals, saved registers, return address. Managed by prologue/epilogue.
concepts.why: Mechanism for function call state. Calling convention (cdecl, fastcall, AAPCS) defines layout. ABI dictates which registers are caller-saved vs callee-saved.

concepts.name: calling_convention
concepts.definition: Contract for function calls: which registers hold arguments, where return value goes, which registers must be preserved.
concepts.why: Inter-function compatibility. x86_64 System V: first 6 integer args in registers; return in RAX. ABI compatibility lets binaries from different compilers interoperate. Violation = crash.

concepts.name: ABI_application_binary_interface
concepts.definition: Set of conventions: calling convention, struct layout, name mangling, exception handling format. Lets compiled code interoperate.
concepts.why: ABI stability is what lets shared libraries work. Different ABIs (Microsoft x64 vs System V) make Windows-Linux binary compat hard. C++'s name mangling is part of its ABI; ABI breakage is a big deal.

concepts.name: code_generation
concepts.definition: Final step: produce assembly or machine code from optimised IR. Includes instruction selection, register allocation, scheduling, emission.
concepts.why: Where IR becomes the artifact users actually run. Quality bridges 'optimised algorithm' and 'actual performance'. Compiler back-end engineering = code gen quality.

rules.name: lexer_parser_split_separates_concerns
if: lexer handles regular tokens; parser handles context-free structure
then: each stage can be designed and tested independently
rules.why: Tokens have no nested structure (regular); programs do (CFG). Separating them lets the lexer be a fast DFA + parser focus on grammar. Universal design pattern in front-ends.

rules.name: recursive_descent_for_LL_grammars
if: grammar is LL(k) for small k
then: hand-written recursive descent is practical and gives best error messages
rules.why: One function per non-terminal mirrors grammar structure. Error messages can be tailored per non-terminal. Clang, Rust, Go all use recursive-descent parsers. Generated LR parsers struggle with error recovery.

rules.name: HM_inference_complete_for_let_polymorphism
if: language has prenex polymorphism via let-bindings and no subtyping
then: Hindley-Milner inference is complete (finds principal types)
rules.why: Damas-Milner theorem: for HM type system, every expression has a most general type; the algorithm finds it. Extensions (subtyping, higher-rank polymorphism) break completeness.

rules.name: unification_finds_most_general_substitution
if: two types can be unified
then: unification algorithm finds the most general substitution making them equal
rules.why: Robinson's theorem. Most-general = applying it loses minimum constraint information. Lets HM defer commitments until necessary; combine with let-generalisation to recover polymorphism.

rules.name: alias_analysis_precision_enables_more_optimisation
if: alias analysis can prove two memory operations target disjoint locations
then: they can be reordered / parallelised / eliminated
rules.why: Conservative aliasing forbids reordering — compilers must assume the worst. Precise alias analysis unlocks: instruction reordering, loop vectorisation, dead store elimination. Quality of alias analysis directly determines downstream optimisation quality.

rules.name: escape_analysis_enables_stack_allocation
if: an object's lifetime doesn't escape its allocation scope
then: it can be stack-allocated, eliminating GC pressure
rules.why: Stack is essentially free. Heap allocations cost the allocator + future GC. Escape analysis proves the object dies with the scope; stack allocation valid. Java + Go + V8 all exploit this aggressively.

rules.name: loop_vectorisation_requires_no_dependencies
if: loop iterations are independent
then: vectorisation gives Nx speedup proportional to SIMD width
rules.why: Dependencies (output of iteration k feeds input of k+1) prevent parallel execution. Auto-vectorisers detect this via alias + dependence analysis. When proof fails, no vectorisation (or scalar epilogue handles overlap).

rules.name: register_allocation_quality_dominates_back_end_performance
if: the back-end emits code with poor register allocation
then: generated code has frequent spills + memory accesses
rules.why: Each spill is a memory access — ~4 cycles vs 0 for register. Hot loops with bad RA can be 5-10x slower than well-allocated equivalents. Spilling is the central problem of code gen.

rules.name: graph_coloring_RA_optimal_with_K_colors
if: interference graph is K-colorable
then: all live ranges fit in physical registers without spilling
rules.why: K = number of registers; coloring with K colors means no two interfering values use the same register. K-colorability is NP-hard in general; spilling handles uncoverable cases.

rules.name: linear_scan_trades_quality_for_speed
if: compilation time matters (JIT context)
then: linear scan RA's O(n log n) beats graph coloring's super-linear cost
rules.why: JITs compile while the program waits. Graph coloring is too slow even at moderate function sizes. Linear scan gives ~10% worse code but compiles 5-10x faster. Used in V8, LuaJIT, .NET.

rules.name: instruction_selection_optimal_via_DP_on_DAG
if: instruction patterns have costs assigned
then: BURS finds the minimum-cost tiling of the IR DAG
rules.why: Dynamic programming on DAG: each node's min cost is the min over its possible cover patterns. Classic technique; LLVM's SelectionDAG, GCC's RTL both variants of this approach.

rules.name: method_JIT_amortises_compilation_over_repeated_execution
if: a function is called many times
then: JIT compilation overhead is amortised across calls
rules.why: Compile-once, run-many. JVM HotSpot compiles a method only after ~10K invocations — by then, the compilation cost is negligible per call. Cold code stays interpreted; hot code is compiled aggressively.

rules.name: tracing_JIT_specialises_to_observed_path
if: a trace is recorded through hot code
then: compilation specialises to that exact path
rules.why: Strong inlining across the trace's calls. No virtual dispatch — observed receiver types are baked in. The cost: trace exits (guards) deoptimise back to interpreter if reality diverges from the recorded path.

rules.name: tiered_compilation_balances_latency_and_steady_state
if: a JIT supports multiple tiers
then: cheap tier optimises startup; expensive tier optimises steady state
rules.why: C1 in HotSpot compiles quickly with modest optimisation; C2 spends 10x more time for maximum quality. Promotion based on call count. The dominant pattern in production JITs since the 2010s.

rules.name: OSR_required_for_hot_loops_in_cold_functions
if: a function contains a hot loop but the function is rarely called
then: OSR is required to transition the running loop to optimised code
rules.why: Without OSR, the loop runs interpreted forever (the function's call count is too low to trigger compilation). OSR copies interpreter state to optimised stack frame mid-execution. Tricky but critical for JIT performance on long-running computations.

rules.name: inline_caches_specialise_dynamic_dispatch
if: a virtual call site sees consistent receiver type
then: inline cache resolves the call in O(1)
rules.why: Generic virtual dispatch: vtable lookup. IC: direct call to cached target after type check. V8, HotSpot, Smalltalk all use this. The mechanism that makes dynamic languages perform: monomorphism is the common case.

rules.name: speculative_optimisation_requires_deoptimisation
if: JIT speculatively optimises based on runtime assumption
then: it must support deoptimisation if the assumption fails
rules.why: Aggressive opts (assume monomorphic call, assume loop iterates many times) can be wrong. Without deopt, wrong code would execute. Deopt: reconstruct interpreter state from compiled state, resume there. The fundamental safety net of speculation.

rules.name: MLIR_dialects_enable_multi_level_optimisation
if: a compiler has IRs at multiple abstraction levels
then: MLIR dialects provide a uniform framework for them
rules.why: Each dialect captures domain-specific structure (linalg for matrix ops, affine for loops, gpu for kernel launches). Lowering progressively rewrites high to low. Shared infrastructure: type system, pass manager, debug info. Used by TensorFlow XLA, PyTorch Inductor.

rules.name: PGO_replaces_compile_time_guesses
if: a compiler has runtime profile data
then: PGO replaces heuristic guesses with measurements
rules.why: Without PGO: 'inline this if it's small'. With PGO: 'inline this — it's called 10M times/sec'. Branch layout, function ordering, inlining all benefit. 5-25% speedup typical; required for max performance.

rules.name: ABI_stability_enables_dynamic_linking
if: compiled libraries follow a stable ABI
then: they can be loaded + linked without recompilation
rules.why: Shared libraries (.so, .dll) depend on this. Calling convention + struct layout + name mangling must match the library's. C ABI is famously stable; C++ ABI has breaking changes (GCC 5 std::string). Rust has no stable ABI by design.
